model_notes: DEEP CYCLICAL AT A TROUGH: FY2020-FY2022 were COVID loss years; a 2022 recapitalisation nearly tripled the share count (1,123M -> 3,368M). Per-share and equity/EPS CAGR history before FY2022 is NOT comparable and equity CAGR is not used as the growth driver.

FY2025 NPAT was NZ$126M; FY2026 guidance (May 2026) is a pre-tax LOSS of NZ$340-390M driven by a jet-fuel price shock (Middle East conflict) plus continued Pratt & Whitney GTF / Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engine groundings of up to ~11 aircraft (~20% of the jet fleet). H1 FY2026 actual was a NZ$59M pre-tax loss / ~NZ$40M net loss.

The DCF base year is NOT FY2025 or guided FY2026. A mid-cycle owner-FCF path is built from FY2025 revenue ($6,755M) forward using component margins that trough in FY2026 (reflecting guided loss) and recover to a normalized, competition-adjusted maturity by ~FY2033-35 (Year 8-10), once engine groundings resolve (management guides substantial resolution by CY2027) and fuel normalizes.

Mature EBITDA margin is capped at ~18.5% (base), below the pre-COVID FY2015-19 average of ~24%, to reflect structurally higher competition from Jetstar's NZ/Tasman expansion (announced 2025) eroding the ~82% domestic monopoly economics, plus a persistently higher cost base (engineering, levies).

Airline capex is lumpy: committed fleet-renewal capex (10x Boeing 787s FY2026-29, A321neo, ATR deliveries) keeps capex elevated (12-14.5% of revenue) through the explicit build before tapering to a normalized maintenance level (~9% of revenue) once the fleet-renewal programme completes around Year 6-7.

Engine-manufacturer compensation (NZ$129M FY2025, NZ$55M H1 FY2026) is a one-off/negotiated support item partially offsetting grounding costs; it is NOT built into the recurring mid-cycle FCF base (treated as noise around the trough, not a repeatable cash flow).

Net debt uses the CSV TotalDebt (gross interest-bearing debt incl. lease liabilities, $2,838M) less Cash & Equivalents ($1,436M) = $1,402M. The company's own narrower net-debt metric (which also nets interest-bearing assets/derivatives) is lower at $1,080M FY2025; the more conservative CSV-based net debt is used throughout.

BEAR CASE WARNING: under the bear scenario (fuel stays elevated, Jetstar erodes domestic margin, groundings persist), the DCF enterprise value falls below current net debt, implying a mechanically negative per-share equity value. This is not a modelling error - it reflects the genuine equity-wipeout / dilutive-recapitalisation tail risk flagged in the qualitative bear case (another equity raise). The bear intrinsic value is floored at a nominal NZ$0.02/share for display and probability-weighting purposes; the raw (negative) DCF output is retained in valuation.bear.raw_intrinsic_value for transparency.

10-year explicit horizon used (not 5) because owner-FCF margins are still well below maturity in Year 5 across all scenarios - capitalizing an immature Year-5 margin via Gordon growth would systematically understate the business coming out of the current trough.

inputs.interest_income_strip_rationale: Air NZ is a net-debt company (net debt $1,402M > FCF base) - interest income is left inside FCF per the standard rule (strip only when net CASH is material). No double-count risk here.
inputs.sbc_source: AIR.NZ_Metrics.csv (StockBasedComp + EquityAwardTaxes columns), immaterial for an airline (~0.16% of revenue)
inputs.gearing_note: FY2025 net debt/EBITDA (company definition) = 1.1x, within the 1.5x-2.5x Capital Management Framework target range but expected to rise given the guided FY2026 loss. Gearing (Net Debt/(Net Debt+Equity), company definition) = 35.7% FY2025.

historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: Standard CAGR-based growth selection is NOT used for this ticker. FY2020-22 COVID losses and the 2022 recapitalisation (share count 1,123M->3,368M) make revenue/equity/EPS/FCF CAGRs across that window not economically meaningful (e.g. revenue 3yr CAGR of 35.2% is a COVID-recovery base effect, not sustainable growth; EPS and FCF CAGRs are undefined or distorted by negative/near-zero base years). The DCF instead builds mid-cycle owner-FCF directly from FY2025 revenue using component margins (EBITDA/SBC/D&A/tax/capex/working-capital) that ramp from a guided FY2026 trough to a competition-adjusted mature level by Year 8-10. See model_notes.
historical_growth.notes: Pre-COVID (FY2015-19) NPAT margin averaged ~7.0% on ~1,123M shares; FY2023 (post-recap, pre-engine-crisis) NPAT margin was 6.5%, the best recent-era mid-cycle anchor. FY2024/25 NPAT margins (2.2%/1.9%) are depressed by the engine-availability crisis (~$165m FY25 EBT impact) and are treated as a Year-1/Year-2 trough, not the steady state.

base.scenario_narrative: Mid-cycle recovery by FY2028-29: engine groundings substantially resolve (per management CY2027 guidance), fuel normalizes from the 2026 Middle East-driven spike, Jetstar competition caps but does not destroy the domestic margin, fleet renewal (787-9s/A321neos) completes and lowers unit costs.

bull.scenario_narrative: Faster engine resolution, fleet-driven capacity growth resumes, Jetstar incursion contained to competitive-but-manageable, dividends/buybacks resume at scale.

bear.scenario_narrative: Fuel stays structurally elevated, Jetstar domestic incursion compresses the monopoly margin persistently, engine groundings drag into FY2028, cost-out only partially offsets. EV falls below current net debt in this scenario, implying material equity-wipeout / further-raise risk (see model_notes).

build_up.component: NZ mid-cap risk-free + equity risk premium base
build_up.note: Starting point for an NZX mid-cap industrial/transport name
Airlines swing from profit to large loss on fuel/demand shocks within a single year (FY24 EBT $222m -> FY25 $189m -> FY26 guided -$340 to -$390m)
USD-denominated fuel and lease/debt costs vs NZD revenue; 2026 Middle East fuel shock (US$85-90/bbl to US$160-230/bbl) demonstrates the tail risk
Multi-year, largely uncontrollable GTF/Trent 1000 grounding issue (up to 20% of jet fleet) with repeatedly-extended resolution timelines (2026 pushed to 2027)

~51% Crown ownership provided a real COVID-era recapitalisation backstop; Baa1 (Moody's) rating - one of the highest-rated airlines globally - reduces funding-cost and solvency tail risk versus an unrated/junk peer, partially offsetting the cyclicality premium

wacc_rationale.bear_wacc_note: Bear WACC carries an additional dilution/recapitalisation-risk premium given the scenario explicitly contemplates another equity raise.

bear.intrinsic_value_note: Raw DCF output is negative (equity value < 0), reflecting equity-wipeout / further-capital-raise risk under this scenario. Floored at a nominal NZ$0.02/share for display and probability-weighting - NOT a literal price target.

sensitivity.note: Matrix uses the base-case owner-FCF path (10yr) with terminal cap of 13x Year-10 FCF; rows = WACC, columns = terminal growth

probability_weighted.note: Bear scenario intrinsic value uses the floored NZ$0.02/share figure (not the raw negative DCF output) for this blend, since a negative per-share value is not economically interpretable in a weighted average.

current_multiples.historical_ev_ebitda_range_note: Air NZ has historically traded around 3-5x EV/EBITDA; current EV/EBITDA of ~3.0x (on FY2025 EBITDA) sits at the low end, consistent with the market already pricing significant distress (FY2026 guided loss, engine crisis, fuel shock).
